title: A Prayer Heard in Dwaraka
subtitle: How Draupadi's prayer crossed the miles to Krishna's side
story:
In Dwaraka, Krishna lay asleep with Rukmini resting by his side. In the Kamyaka forest, far away, Draupadi's heart was failing her. And at that very moment ten thousand ascetics were walking toward the Pandavas' hermitage.

The sage Durvasa had timed his visit carefully. He had first ascertained that the Pandavas were all seated at their ease and that Draupadi had finished her meal and was reposing; then, surrounded by ten thousand disciples, he repaired to the forest. Yudhishthira, seeing such a guest arrive, went forward to receive him, joined his palms, pointed to an excellent seat, and gave the rishis a fit and respectful welcome. "Return quick, O adorable sir," he said, "after performing thy diurnal ablutions and observances." And the sinless muni, not troubling himself to wonder how the king would provide a feast for him and his disciples, went with them to the stream to bathe.

But Draupadi, devoted to her husbands, was in great anxiety about the food. The vessel that fed the Pandavas was a gift of the sun: it remained full until she had finished her meal, and empty after. She had already eaten. There was no food in it now, and no way of filling it — and a guest like Durvasa could not be turned away with apologies.

After much anxious thought, she came to the conclusion that there were no means of providing a feast. And so she did what she had done in her darkest hour before: she prayed. Inwardly, to Krishna, the slayer of Kamsa. "Krishna, O Krishna, of mighty arms, O son of Devaki, whose power is inexhaustible," she said in her heart, "thou art the soul, the creator and the destroyer of the universe, the saviour of the afflicted, ever kindly disposed towards those that take refuge in thee — thou with a complexion dark as the leaves of the blue lotus, eyes red as the corolla of the lily, attired in yellow robes, with the bright Kaustubha gem in thy bosom. As thou didst protect me before from Dussasana, do thou extricate me now from this difficulty."

The great and sovereign God, lord of the earth, of mysterious movements, ever kind to those who depend on him, heard her. Perceiving her difficulty, he instantly repaired to that place — leaving the bed of Rukmini, who slept on unaware.

Draupadi bowed down to him in great joy and told him everything: the arrival of the munis, the empty vessel, her fear of the sage's wrath. And Krishna, who had crossed half the world at the thought of her trouble, said only: "I am very much afflicted with hunger. Do thou give me some food without delay, and then thou mayst go about thy work."

She was confused. "The sun-given vessel remains full till I finish my meal," she said. "But I have already taken my meal today; there is no food in it now."

"This is no time for jest," said Krishna. "I am much distressed with hunger. Go thou quickly, fetch the vessel, and show it to me."

She had the vessel brought, and he looked into it and saw a particle of rice and vegetable sticking at its rim. He took it and swallowed it. "May it please the god Hari, the soul of the universe," he said, "and may that god who partaketh at sacrifices be satiated with this."

Then the long-armed Krishna, the soother of miseries, said to Bhimasena: "Do thou speedily invite the munis to dinner." And Bhima went quickly to the nearest stream of transparent, cool water — where Durvasa and his disciples, having plunged in, were rubbing their bodies and finding, to their astonishment, that their stomachs were full to the throat. They came out of the water and stared at one another. "Having bade the king make our meals ready, we have come hither for a bath," they said. "But how can we eat anything now? The repast hath been uselessly prepared for us."

And Durvasa, understanding at last, said: "By spoiling the repast, we have done a great wrong to that royal sage, king Yudhishthira."
reflection: The story's hinge is that Draupadi's prayer is answered before it finishes: Krishna leaves Rukmini's bed in Dwaraka the instant the thought forms in the forest. And the miracle is rendered with almost comic smallness — not a feast conjured from the sky, but one leftover grain swallowed at the rim of an empty pot, after which the world quietly rearranges itself. Krishna's protection here is not spectacle; it is presence, arriving exactly when there was no other help.
tradition_note: The sun-given vessel that fed the Pandavas until Draupadi had eaten is the same vessel the epic elsewhere calls the Akshaya-patra, and Durvasa's visit is one of several episodes that turn on its power.
next_story_tease: Now Durvasa and his disciples had to face the king whose feast their own bellies had already consumed.
hero_scene: Krishna in yellow robes arriving at the forest hermitage at dusk, Draupadi bowing before him in joy, while in the distance the ascetics bathe in the stream — and behind them, unseen, the empty vessel with a single grain at its rim.
